=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Buyer’s position

**Do not accept this package as settled.** The Seller’s “[STANDARD]” labels and “Reviewer Efficiency Note” are not evidence of Buyer agreement. Several supposedly standard provisions would materially weaken Wattlebridge’s remedies or leave it acquiring unresolved debt, contractual and IP risks.

This review is based on the supplied extracts, not the full SPA or underlying DD documents. References to those documents need verification.

## Material issues and pushback

### 1. Liability limitations would undermine the protections being negotiated

**Seller position:** A 20% general warranty cap (AUD 4.8 million), AUD 25,000 de minimis, AUD 250,000 deductible basket and 18-month notification period; broader language extends limitations to all Claims. Capacity and title receive the same treatment.

**Why it matters:** The combined effect is more important than any individual number. Buyer could suffer a substantial loss yet recover little—or nothing. Applying the package to “all Claims” may also restrict debt repayment obligations, purchase-price adjustments, tax claims and specific indemnities. A title defect could jeopardise the entire AUD 24 million investment while recovery remains capped at AUD 4.8 million.

**Push back:**
- Confine the general regime to clearly defined **general warranty claims**, with express precedence for carve-outs throughout clauses 9.3, 12, 13 and 20.5.
- Seek a higher general cap and a longer claim period, covering at least two full audit cycles. The current package is a negotiation proposal, not an accepted market standard.
- Seek a lower de minimis, aggregation of related claims and a **tipping basket**—once crossed, qualifying losses are recoverable from the first dollar.
- Give capacity, title and share-ownership warranties a separate cap of at least the purchase price, no de minimis/basket, and a materially longer claim period.
- Establish separate treatment for tax, specific indemnities, payment obligations and price adjustments; preserve fraud remedies and rights that cannot lawfully be excluded.
- Check claim-notice requirements and any deadline to commence proceedings. Timely notified contingent claims should survive pending quantification.

### 2. Disclosure, knowledge and non-reliance provisions could hollow out warranties

**Seller position:** Everything in or referred to in the data room and public records is disclosed; Buyer loses claims for matters known to Buyer or advisers, including anything “discoverable”. Exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply broadly.

**Why it matters:** This effectively transfers the risk of buried, incomplete or ambiguous information to Buyer. “Discoverable” goes beyond actual knowledge. Coupled with non-reliance and exclusive remedies, it could remove alternative recourse while leaving little warranty protection.

**Push back:**
- Require **fair disclosure with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the matter**, preferably against the relevant warranty.
- Reject blanket disclosure of public registers, documents merely “referred to”, and unrestricted data-room contents. If any general disclosure remains, tightly define it and preserve a frozen, indexed copy.
- Delete constructive/imputed knowledge and adviser knowledge. If a knowledge exclusion is unavoidable, limit it to actual knowledge of named Buyer deal-team members.
- Preserve specific indemnities and completion obligations **despite disclosure or knowledge**.
- Narrow exclusive remedies and non-reliance provisions, preserving express contractual protections, appropriate equitable relief, fraud and non-excludable statutory rights.
- Require disclosure updates through Completion, without automatic acceptance or waiver of new matters.

The letter’s reservation that it admits no breach does not resolve the underlying risks. Equally, disclosure of uncertainty is not proof that a breach has occurred.

### 3. Bluefen consent is a critical completion condition, not an endeavours obligation

Bluefen represents approximately **30% of FY26 revenue (AUD 3.6 million)**. No final written consent or evidence of satisfaction of its associated conditions has been supplied.

**Why it matters:** Delivery of a consent document alone may not satisfy clause 11.3 or prevent adverse amendments, fees or termination exposure.

**Push back:** Make effective Bluefen change-control consent, with all associated conditions satisfied and no adverse variation without Buyer approval, a **Buyer-waivable condition precedent**. Require the underlying documents and evidence of effectiveness. Include a longstop date and Buyer termination right. Reasonable endeavours may govern the Seller’s efforts; it must not replace the required outcome.

### 4. Riverlark must be discharged at Completion

Approximately **AUD 3.2 million** remains outstanding. A release “following Completion” leaves Buyer exposed to secured debt and change-control consequences.

**Push back:**
- Obtain a binding payout letter covering principal, interest, fees and all secured obligations.
- Pay the lender directly through the completion funds flow from the appropriate Seller proceeds.
- Require effective releases of security and relevant guarantees at Completion, with controlled undertakings for subsequent registry filings where necessary.
- Confirm no residual facilities, security or change-control default survives.

Reconcile the AUD 24 million price to the agreed debt-free/cash-free mechanics: debt must not remain with Buyer **or be deducted twice** through both the adjustment and funds flow.

### 5. Ironquay presents an ownership risk, not merely an unpaid invoice

Transfer of SOW3 materials depends on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. AUD 180,000 is recorded as open, but that is not conclusive proof of non-payment. No receipt or confirmatory assignment is available.

**Why it matters:** An indemnity limited to the SOW3 payment may cover the invoice but not the loss arising from missing rights to important software or other materials.

**Push back:**
- Verify all SOW3 amounts and payment status.
- Require cleared payment and an effective confirmatory assignment/release by Completion, with chain-of-title verification.
- Determine how important the materials are to the business; make satisfactory resolution a completion condition if critical.
- Expand the specific indemnity to losses arising from the pre-Completion payment/ownership defect, including reasonable defence and remediation costs—not merely AUD 180,000.
- Give that indemnity an appropriate separate cap, duration and claims regime, unaffected by disclosure or knowledge.

### 6. Completion bonuses need express economic allocation

The **AUD 420,000** conditional bonuses are absent from the funds flow. Payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs remain unresolved.

**Why it matters:** Calling these a “matter for the Seller” does not prevent the Company, and therefore Buyer economically, from bearing them after Completion.

**Push back:** Verify who owes the amounts, the employment conditions and payment timing. Allocate Seller transaction-related bonuses and applicable on-costs expressly to Seller through payment, a price deduction or an appropriately secured indemnity. Address amounts becoming payable after Completion and avoid double counting in debt or working-capital adjustments.

### 7. Export/privacy incident needs investigation and allocated risk

The preliminary record concerns a link sent to an unintended external recipient, potentially covering **approximately 1,240 records**. Access, scope and notification requirements are unconfirmed.

**Why it matters:** The Seller’s “not expected to be material” statement is unsupported. Conversely, the available information does not establish a confirmed notifiable breach or a quantified loss.

**Push back:**
- Require prompt investigation, preservation of logs, containment and a documented assessment of access, data scope and applicable notification duties.
- Check contractual notification requirements as well as applicable privacy law.
- Require updates and appropriate cooperation on remediation and legally required notices.
- Seek a specific indemnity for losses attributable to the pre-Completion incident, including investigation, remediation and third-party claims, with legally recoverable regulatory amounts addressed expressly.
- Consider escrow and a completion protection proportionate to the investigation findings.

### 8. Supplier renewals require substance-based review

Three related renewals total **AUD 330,000**. The letter does not establish that they are ordinary-course, unavoidable, accrued or terminable.

**Push back:** Review DD-008 and DD-011 together for execution dates, service periods, termination rights and commercial necessity. Apply interim operating covenants and consent thresholds on an aggregated basis.

Do not automatically classify the whole AUD 330,000 as debt or leakage: treatment depends on whether these are accrued liabilities, prepayments, ordinary future operating costs or unauthorised commitments. Allocate them consistently with the agreed price mechanics.

### 9. Tax and IP should not be treated as “settled”

**Tax:** Seek a separate pre-Completion tax indemnity/covenant, with appropriate exclusions preventing double recovery, a separate cap and a claim period aligned with relevant assessment/reassessment periods plus a buffer. Eighteen months and general warranty thresholds are inadequate protection for potentially latent tax exposure.

**IP:** Review ownership, contractor and employee assignments, licensing, infringement and relevant third-party dependencies. Ironquay should not be treated as the only possible IP issue. Given the business, consider enhanced protection for core IP rather than automatically accepting the general regime.

### 10. Title evidence and other contract requirements need targeted verification

- **Share title:** DD-012’s register is relevant evidence, not complete verification. Confirm issued capital, valid issuance, beneficial ownership, encumbrances, options/convertibles and transfer restrictions. Require transfers, necessary approvals and registration of Buyer as holder of 100%, supported by fundamental warranties.
- **Office lease:** The supplied description identifies a **notification obligation**, not landlord consent. Check the full lease and require timely compliant notice; do not invent a consent requirement.
- **Mossvale:** An assignment restriction does **not by itself** require consent for a share sale. Check for separate change-control, deemed-assignment or termination provisions before demanding consent.

## Recommended negotiation priorities

1. **Protect Completion:** effective Bluefen consent; Riverlark payout and release; verified clean share title; satisfactory resolution of material Ironquay ownership concerns.
2. **Protect the economics:** reconcile the debt-free/cash-free funds flow and expressly allocate bonuses, on-costs and properly classified supplier liabilities.
3. **Preserve meaningful recourse:** remove blanket “all Claims” limitations, constructive knowledge and indiscriminate disclosure; separate fundamental, tax and specific-indemnity protection.
4. **Resolve known uncertainties:** investigate the incident, verify IP payment/assignment and obtain the underlying DD documents.
5. **Secure recovery:** assess Seller covenant strength and seek escrow, retention or a guarantee where needed. A strong indemnity has limited value if Seller distributes the proceeds and cannot pay.

**Bottom line:** Do not exchange completion certainty or effective remedies for the Seller’s assertions that matters are “standard”, “addressed” or “settled”. Those conclusions are not supported by the documents supplied.
